entries.title: Local checks, cloud training: what the first measurements cost
entries.text:
The two machines have different jobs. The Apple M1 handles development and FP64/native MuJoCo checks. A rented Runpod Community GPU handles large FP32 training batches; checkpoints and videos return to the Mac for review.

The local diagnostic reached 8,000 samples in 4 h 28 min. A straight-line projection puts 512,000 near 12 days. A Community RTX 3090 reached 122,880 in 27 min 6 s—about 150× faster—and its successful rental cost roughly $0.16.

For 512,000 samples, expect about 1 h 53 min of pure training or 2–2.5 hours including setup and reviews. At prices seen during these tests, that is roughly $0.32–$0.55 on the preferred GPUs. These are September 2026 project estimates, not a Runpod quote. Cloud FP32 is for learning; local FP64 is the quality check.

rows: No rental; preflight, debugging and quality checks

entries.title: Learning to walk: first, learn to leave the floor
entries.text:
A step is a sequence: shift weight, unload one foot, lift it, place it and catch the body. The first policies found safer shortcuts instead—turning or sliding their feet without actually stepping.

Even after rewarding foot clearance up to 3 cm, two 20-second reviews measured zero liftoffs and zero single-leg support. A scripted test confirmed that the pose is kinematically possible, but the simulated actuators saturated before completing the movement.

Weight transfer also exposed forearm–thigh collisions. Opening the arms by 5° removed them; the walking reference now uses 10° with a small penalty below 5°. The clips show failed attempts and diagnostics, not a learned gait. All results are simulation-only.

videos.caption: Round 1, 48,640 samples — a six-second excerpt after the forward command begins. The policy changes foot angles but does not establish a step.
Round 2, 81,920 samples — another six-second excerpt. Automated review measured zero liftoffs and zero single-support states during the full trial.
Scripted load-transfer diagnostic—not a policy. It requests a weight shift and 3 cm foot lift; the dynamic response saturates and does not complete the planned motion.
Round 3, 40,960 samples — the original 0.34-second rollout slowed 5×. It terminates on unintended contact before the walking command starts.

images.caption: Left to right: the same weight-transfer pose with arms at 0°, 5° and 10° outward. Red marks a forearm–thigh proxy contact at 0°; both wider settings are clear.

entries.title: Collision geometry: why Manfred now uses 30 hand-built boxes
entries.text:
A robot simulation uses two representations of the same machine: a detailed model for display, and simpler shapes for calculating contact with the ground and between body parts. These collision shapes determine where the simulator allows contact—not just where it draws the robot.

Detailed geometry costs more to check, especially across repeated training steps. Simpler geometry is cheaper, but must preserve important clearances: oversized shapes create false collisions, while undersized ones can miss real contact. Manfred’s feet therefore use a sole and two side walls, preserving the space inside.

Automatically generated boxes were initially too bulky. Refining them with smaller shapes and convex meshes improved the fit, but made contact calculations expensive: one compilation was killed by the system, and another took about 18 minutes. Further automatic simplification reintroduced false contacts.

The project owner instead built 30 boxes manually in Fusion, choosing their dimensions, orientation and placement around the relevant parts. The software stack, visual model, masses and joints remain unchanged. Visual alignment and ankle-roll checks have been accepted. The new model has 394 contact pairs, none involving meshes; its performance still needs measuring.

Below: the detailed robot as a reference, followed by three collision models. All use the same pose, camera and lighting.

images.caption: Visual reference. The detailed CAD model, with collision geometry hidden.
1. Automatic coarse boxes. Simple, but bulky around the upper body. This early version did not include the foot side walls.
2. Automatic refined shapes. A closer fit, using boxes and convex meshes—but more expensive contact calculations.
3. Thirty manual Fusion boxes. Simple shapes placed deliberately, with tilted lower-leg boxes and space between the foot walls.

entries.title: Learn in a computer. Use the same skill in a robot.
entries.text:
First, a simulated Manfred practises standing. The training program scores each attempt and changes how it chooses movements. After many attempts, it has a learned skill, called a policy. It is not a movie of movements: the policy chooses what to do from what the robot senses right now. Using the trained policy does not keep training it.

ONNX saves that skill in a file. The exact same file can run in simulation and on the real robot, without changing the policy. That is the plan for Manfred: one policy file for both, with matching inputs and outputs.

The robot repeats a simple loop 50 times a second: read its joint positions and balance sensors, let the policy choose target joint angles, send those targets to the motor controller, then read again.

The goal is to keep this loop the same for a simulated robot and a real one. Only the connection underneath changes: one reads simulated sensors and moves simulated motors; the other talks to real electronics. The policy should not need to ask which robot it controls.

The ONNX policy has now kept Manfred standing for 30 seconds in standard MuJoCo. Real hardware still needs calibration and safety testing.

entries.title: Finding the limit: 10° and 15° tilted starts
entries.text: Manfred’s trained standing policy tries to return to its upright reference pose. With no retraining, it recovered in all four tested directions from 10° starts. At 15°, it fell forward/backward or made contact between its legs during sideways trials. These are tilted starts, not pushes, in MuJoCo/MJX—not hardware tests. Clips compare forward and leftward starts; failed trials end early.

videos.caption: 15° forward — fell; trial terminated after 1.02 s.
10° leftward — recovered; feet reposition during recovery.
15° leftward — contact between the legs; trial terminated after 0.16 s.

entries.title: Push recovery: 1 N, 3 N, 5 N
entries.text: Manfred recovered from 1 N and 3 N pushes in all four directions, but fell at 5 N. Each push lasted 0.2 s; the policy was unchanged. These MuJoCo/MJX results describe this test only—not hardware readiness. Videos below show backward pushes, applied at 5 seconds.

videos.caption: 3 N / 0.2 s — recovered after a larger tilt.
5 N / 0.2 s — fell; recording ends when the trial terminates.
